transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's just that everything feels so heavy lately, you know? I mean, what brings me in is that I've just completely stopped wanting to do the things that usually keep me going. And I'm a guy who usually has a lot going on. I've been a carpenter for over thirty years, and usually, just walking into my shop—even on a Sunday when I'm not working—just taking a deep breath and smelling the sawdust, the pine, the oak... that usually centers me. But lately? I walk in there and I feel absolutely nothing. I don't even want to turn the lights on. 

And it's not just work. I used to go to salsa nights every Thursday down at the community center. I’m not the best dancer, but I love the energy, the music, the people. I haven't been in weeks. The thought of getting dressed and going out just feels impossible. Same with church gatherings on Sundays. I usually help set up the chairs, pour the coffee, chat with everyone... but I’ve been making up excuses not to go. I even stopped cooking for my neighbors. I used to make this big batch of chili or smoke some ribs and just bring plates over to the folks next door, just to be neighborly. But now... I barely even want to make a sandwich for myself. It's like the color has just drained out of everything I used to love doing, and I just don't understand why I can't snap out of it.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, lately?

Well, yes. Yes, I have. It's... it's practically every day now, and it usually starts right when I open my eyes. Most mornings, I wake up and before my feet even hit the floor, there's just this... this incredibly heavy, hollow feeling sitting right here in my chest. It's almost physical, you know? Like a weight. And I look around our bedroom—the room my wife and I have shared for twenty years, the one I painted that nice warm yellow so it would feel bright—and it just looks gray. Like all the color has just been completely sucked out of the house. 

And then I have to just lay there for a minute and gather myself, because my wife, Mary, she's usually already awake, reading her book or getting ready, and I have to put on a brave face. I have to force myself, really force myself, to hold it together so I don't just completely break down in front of her. She’s a worrier, Mary is. If she sees me crying or looking like the world is ending, she’ll fuss over me all day, and I just can't bear to put her through that. But keeping it in, acting like I'm just tired or my back hurts from the shop, it takes so much energy. So, yes, doctor, to answer your question, it's pretty much the whole day, every day, starting from the moment I wake up with that awful emptiness.
Have you been feeling fatigued or lacking energy lately, even when you haven’t done anything physically demanding?

Oh, absolutely. It's... it's honestly one of the most frustrating parts of whatever this is. Because, like I said, I'm a carpenter, I'm used to hard, physical labor. I know exactly what a tired body is supposed to feel like. But this? This is entirely different. I can get a full night's sleep—I mean, eight or nine solid hours right there in bed—or I could just be sitting down in my La-Z-Boy all afternoon doing absolutely nothing, and my body still feels completely, utterly worn out. 

It feels exactly like I've been framing a roof all day. You know, when you're up there hauling heavy wooden trusses and swinging a hammer for ten hours straight, balancing on the joists, and your muscles are just screaming by the time you finally climb down the ladder? That's the exact, deep ache I have in my bones right now, except I haven't done a lick of work to earn it. 

And it makes the smallest things feel impossible. Just... just normal, everyday small chores. Like loading my tools into the truck. I’ve got this old Ford F-150, and usually, tossing my toolbelt and a couple of circular saws into the back is just muscle memory. Takes two seconds, doesn't even register in my brain as work. But lately, I just stand there in the garage looking at my belt, and the thought of picking it up and walking twenty feet to the driveway... it just feels like too much. It's like I'm trying to move a mountain just to get through a basic chore. I just don't have the gas in the tank for it, doctor, even when I haven't lifted a single finger all day.
Have you noticed that you're moving more slowly than usual, or have others commented that you seem slowed down or restless?

Well, yes, actually. And it's not just me noticing it, it's the guys at the job site, too. My foreman, Dave—we've worked together for, gosh, fifteen years now—he actually pulled me aside the other day. He asked if I was feeling okay, because he said I was moving like my work boots were filled with wet cement. And he's right. Just... just bending down to pick up a two-by-four feels like it takes me ten minutes. I have to think about moving my arm, think about gripping the wood, think about standing back up. Every single movement is just so incredibly slow and deliberate. It's like I'm moving underwater. 

But then, on the flip side of that, there are times when I can't seem to just stand still, but not in a productive way. I'll be in the shop, and instead of actually cutting the trim or sanding down a cabinet door like I'm supposed to be doing, I just end up pacing. I'll walk from the table saw over to the workbench, then over to the door, then back to the saw, over and over. And I'll just be rubbing my hands together, or picking at the calluses on my thumbs. Dave saw me doing that last Tuesday when we were finishing up a kitchen remodel over in Westlake. He asked what I was looking for, and I didn't even have an answer for him because I wasn't looking for anything. I was just pacing around, completely stuck, not doing a single useful thing. It's embarrassing, really, being a guy who prides himself on his work ethic and efficiency, and now I'm either moving like molasses or walking in circles like a lost dog. It's just not like me at all.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently, like not wanting to eat or losing weight without trying?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I know a lot of folks say they stop eating when they get into a slump, or maybe they eat too much, but for me... it's pretty much been exactly the same. Mary, she still makes us breakfast every morning—usually eggs and toast, maybe some bacon on the weekends—and I sit down at the kitchen table and eat it just like I always have. I don't necessarily enjoy it the way I used to, you know? It all kind of tastes like cardboard lately, just bland and pointless, but I still eat it because it's there and because I know I need fuel for the day, even if I don't end up doing much at the site.

And lunch is the same. I pack my cooler every night—a turkey sandwich on wheat, an apple, maybe a handful of pretzels—and I eat it in the truck around noon. Sometimes I don't finish the apple, but the sandwich always goes down. And then dinner... Mary's a wonderful cook, makes a pot roast that would knock your socks off, and I always clear my plate. I haven't noticed my jeans fitting any looser or tighter, either. I've been wearing the same size 34 Carhartts for the better part of a decade, and I buckle my belt on the exact same notch every single morning. So, no, doctor, my appetite hasn't really changed, and my weight seems to be holding steady right around 185, where it's been since I was in my thirties. It's just... the enjoyment of the food is gone, but the eating itself, that hasn't changed a bit.
Have you been feeling like you’re worthless or guilty about things more than usual?

Yeah. Yeah, I have. A lot, actually. It's... it's heavy, doctor. It just sits right on my chest all day and I can't shake it. 

I mentioned Mary earlier, my wife. She's... well, she's had some health issues lately, and I just... I can't stop thinking about it. I keep replaying every single doctor's appointment we've been to in my head, over and over like a bad movie. Every little change in her health, every time she mentioned feeling off or looking a little pale... I just sit there in my chair at home and analyze it. I think about last fall, when she first said she wasn't feeling quite right, and I just told her she was probably working too hard in the garden. Why did I do that? I just keep telling myself that a better husband would have caught it sooner. A better man would have paid closer attention and protected her somehow, you know? 

I should have insisted she go to the clinic right then and there. Instead, I was probably just complaining about my own tired bones after work, completely oblivious to the woman right in front of me. And now she's going through all this, and I'm just... I'm practically useless to her with the way I've been feeling. I replay the drive to that specialist over in the city, sitting in that freezing waiting room, the look on her face when the doctor came in, and I just think, if I had just been a decent partner six months ago, maybe we wouldn't be in this mess. Maybe I could have stopped it from getting to this point. 

It eats at me. It really does. She's taken care of me for thirty years, packed my lunches, made my dinners, and when she actually needed me to step up and notice something was wrong with her, I failed her. I completely missed it. It makes me feel lower than dirt, to be honest with you. Just completely, utterly worthless as a husband and as a man.
Have you had any thoughts about ending your life or that life isn't worth living?

Well, doctor... it's hard to talk about. It really is. I've always been the kind of guy who just puts his head down and pushes through, you know? But lately, with everything feeling so heavy, and the guilt about Mary, and just... just not being able to do my job the way I used to... my mind goes to some pretty dark places. 

I haven't... I haven't made any plans or anything like that, if that's what you're asking. I wouldn't do that to Mary, especially not now. But I do have these thoughts. Like, I'll be lying in bed at night, staring at the ceiling fan—it's got this little wobble to it that I keep meaning to fix, but I just haven't had the energy—and I'll think to myself... maybe it would just be easier if I didn't wake up tomorrow. If I just went to sleep and that was it. No more feeling like I'm moving through wet cement, no more of this crushing guilt sitting on my chest, no more letting everyone down. Just quiet.

And then, sometimes, it goes a little further than that. I'll be sitting in my truck at the job site, eating that sandwich Mary packed for me, and I'll catch myself thinking that maybe... maybe she and the kids would actually be better off without me. I mean, what good am I doing them right now? I'm a burden. I'm just this miserable, slow, useless lump taking up space in the house. If I wasn't around, maybe Mary could focus on her own health instead of worrying about why I'm pacing around the kitchen or staring blankly at the TV. Maybe they'd get the life insurance money and they'd be fine. They'd be better than fine. 

It scares me, doctor. It really does. Because I love my family more than anything in this world. I've spent thirty years building a life for us, building houses for other people so I could provide for mine. And to have my own brain telling me that they'd be better off if I was dead... it's terrifying. I try to push the thoughts away, I really do. I'll turn on the radio in the truck, or I'll try to focus on the grain of the wood I'm working with, but they just keep creeping back in. Just this constant whisper that life isn't worth all this trouble, and that I'm not worth the trouble I'm causing everyone else.
